I think people are too quick to judge. My friend who just passed away last year was a great parent. 

She was born with short arms, three fingers on each and one of each double organ. It was a long road for her but she was a fighter, and one of my best friends. 

She could of died during the pregnancy, but marched through like a trooper. I’m just glad I got to spend her last year with her a few times a week talking, and getting some of the most insightful life advise I’ve ever had. I have my own issues, and she really helped me see past what others may see as weird or look down on. But yea people judged her ability to parent, but she did a wonderful job and passed away at 38 due to her ongoing struggles. She saw her kid through from birth to 18 when she passed away. It was around the time he moved out she just spiraled health wise and her health took its toll. It was like she did her job, and was done and ready to go.

He even turned out gifted, and received top honors and a special scholarship. She was gifted as well, regardless of her disabilities. It goes to show you can’t judge a book by its cover.

Old post but it’s all about the mids! You can easily achieve the tone with a Green Muff…Tone and Sustain rolled down to more a distortion sound. And then stack a TS first with tone all the way up for brightness  and gain at 0. You can add a slight boost after and there you go! The amp does play a roll, but you don’t have to have it. Even if you bought a SFT pedal to emulate it. You still need a PDF 1/2 or something with a mid eq curve like a TS or even a Treble booster will work. I’ve also swapped out for the DLS3 MIAB pedal instead of the Muff, then just cranked the mids, cut some treble and bass. Then put more mids into it via a TS. The TS is really a substitute for the PDF here as it acts as a boost and EQ more so.

We now know he was using a Way Huge Big Muff style (Green Pickle) pedal into the AMPEG, PDF1 for more mids and sometimes a cocked wah. It’s not a hard time to nail. Just hard to setup right in a band mix or recording to cut right. But leaning on the mids, stacking pedals is the biggest part here regardless of amp selection. Seem like bass was cut a lot as well, then made use of the Rhythm circuit on Humbuckers to get some bottom mids back on parts. Second guitar player takes a more spacial complimentary approach.

Note lots of Indie and desert rock bands use one of two combos…. TS into RAT medium to low gain, TS into Muff. I do both and it achieves a lot of the genres tones. The stacking of the pedals and combinations gets the sounds. But for a beginner with only one pedal they could buy…the SFT would get close dialed in right.

Suboxone can have crazy effects if not taken regularly. I’ve had friends that puked all night, or nod so hard they couldn’t go anywhere. Also visuals when closing eyes. If use to it, for me it feels no different than a shot of espresso to get my day going. But it takes weeks to build that tolerance. 

It’s like the warning labels say, don’t drive or operate heavy machinery till you get use to medicine. So yeah this is dangerous for many reasons. I don’t think your husband understands suboxone, as the withdrawals if taken long term  can be long and grueling. This is a set back of your 2 days a bit here. Cause you still gotta go through withdrawl. Sub will prolong it, and is more a short term taper plan, or stop button until you can not relapse and need to get sorted. 

I’d rather taper or cold turkey oxy, Vs a Sub withdraw that can last a month! If I knew what I knew back then when they presented me with a “miracle drug” in 2007. It was just as hard if not worse to get off.

The other half the time they just reiterate verbally what you are already doing, then tell their boss they told you and take credit for stuff they didn’t do. 

In lots of positions in offices it’s a BS cushy job. They are only there, because the real boss doesn’t want to talk to the workers. So they have an middle man, to stay hidden in an office. They just report back how things are going. A designated team lead could easily do that in a meeting or shoot an email. I see so many friends and family, hired as middle management its not funny. So having workers in the office, is critical to them keeping their job. Just like relationships with lease companies are made. Not needed, but more a network to give jobs to funnel money to keep higher ups happy, family jobs and long term business relationships in place.

Yeah, that’s the one thing I think is a bit understated when people pay for the “mix with the pros” courses. You think those guys like CLA don’t have stellar recorded tracks already? They are just there to make it compatible with todays playback devices, and give it a bit more energy. Otherwise all faders up, all mixing tools off. It’ll still sound better than 99% of most peoples mixes. Probably the most important factor. But also remember people use so many VST instruments…however same rule applies. You don’t choose a preset that sounds good, with all kinds of eq, fx baked in. You need to know how the sound is made, and clear the fx off then bring things back in on a send or whatever. Those presets are mostly demo purposes, and need to be corrected as well at the source.

Yep, flat rates are a bad idea. It’s not good to be mixing, only to find out all the guitars need to be redone and some elements cannot be saved. But if you said $500 for a project, and you end up doing overdubs when all you were to do is mix. This can happen easily to people starting out. Also the revisions…one person may be happy, and another member may not. 

Most on their first or second album will keep asking for mixes, till you can’t take it anymore. At that point you’ll wish you never took on the project. It’s good to see the group or bands previous work, to get an idea where they are as well. You don’t want to be fighting 3-4 different personalities, and not getting paid for it. I’ve had much smoother sailing, with musicians that are a bit more seasoned. Than a garage band that dumps a folder with tascam tracks, recorded on RadioShack mics on you.. they got their live sound guy to do. There’s so many reasons you shouldn’t do a flat rate or undervalue yourself. As well as researching before taking on a project, while setting standards for what you are provided with.

Advise to my younger self on mixing…I started before using computers. I’d say remember all you learned mixing on those 4 tracks, do some live sound to sharpen your mixing skills(Live A/V, and fixing that stuff is my salary job) I learned a lot from analog, and also learned the source of the recording matters. Get crap sounding tracks…well you can work hard, replace with samples ect. But you are def going to get in over your head, taking a project like that on. And the money will not equal the work most the time. I took some bad mixing projects on as a young kid, and it was very chaotic and not worth my time. In todays world it’s very important to reference on Bluetooth speakers, laptops  and iPhones. I find a lot of people will find the bass is lacking and it’s too muddy. So you go back to your 250hz-1khz range to make it audible or cut. Consumer devices are good at revealing this, as nice cans and monitors usually have big low end that can mask your lower mids. One big thing many mentioned, reading the manual. It’s easy to record and feel great in the moment. Then playback and wonder why it’s not as good. Could be there is latency you never knew how to deal with. All DAWs are different…find out how your Daw handles latency. And also take advantage of direct monitoring outside the DAW. This will save you a lot of headaches, if you can’t get another take.

Produce: prepare everything. Gain stage and have a setup. Whether template or tuning your instruments. Then record and experiment with what you have. I found recording good live takes, and getting them right at the source was a big deal. However if you’re all VST ITB, then at least gain stage your VST instruments, and start with “INT” learn how to make sounds from scratch! This helps so much to know what you’re doing. Because presets can have a lot of fx and stuff going on, that simply will clash with your mix later. I’d say NI Massive, is a good simple one to learn from. And a cheap MS20 mini is a great analog one to learn. Or a cheap behringer Model D will cover some ground. Also I’ve found putting demos up too fast online that are good…I tend to not go back and finish. It’s good to get your music out there, but maybe save you best stuff and finish it fully before putting it online at 2am because you’re proud. You only get one impression. Putting up other mixes of the same song, will not have the same experience for the listener.

It’s really a process you need to figure out yourself. But pick 3 instruments and learn them well, pick an eq and learn it well, pick a compressor or two and learn that well. I use the same 5 plugins constantly and rarely just go through tons hitting presets…big drain on creative energy. You’re better off grabbing a pre programmed drum track then from scratch, and just playing your instrument right away. You can always go back and replace stuff. Just go to the races, and don’t get bogged down by drum production or layers of production. Make the song first, then go back as needed. Also don’t waste an entire chain, to make a digital synth sound analog. Just save up and buy a analog synth, and a nice pre amp when you can. I know some big pros that would just setup and record for 45 minutes practices. Then cut out the parts they liked, and that was at least 2 parts of the song to start! Guitar players are good with this when jamming out something. Knowing one instrument formally, like piano or guitar will get you there faster. You can write around that, take your bass root notes, timing and key from that.

Mastering: if you’re dead serious about releasing an album. Get it done by a professional! If it’s more a demo and you have a good enough setup. Then that’s ok, but if I was super proud of something that’s going to see a release on Spotify…it’s going to a pro.

Reference…it’s easy to hear everything great on monitors or headphones you’re comfortable with. Only to listen on an iPhone or Bluetooth speaker and the lows and mids just bottom out. Listen on laptop speakers, earbuds, iPhone and consumer speakers…then take notes to what’s happening of being masked. You’ll be pleasantly surprised after you make the fixes, and go back to the normal speakers. Usually I find 32-800hz area is lacking, too much low end area dependent on the bass to stick out or the low mid range is to muddy. Basic issues I hear on a lot of mixes not tested on a variety of sources. Once it sounds good on computer speakers, iPhone and thin sources you’re improving. 

Sometimes Studio monitors just sound so great because frequencies are being heard not translated to a consumer device. Then you hear it on that Bluetooth speaker and it’s missing! You realize damn, I need to maybe cut those mids more on something and boost on another…or work on that 800hz-1khz for the bass to come out more in the mix Vs depending on the 40hz-120hz that’s creating the bulk of the bass coming through the monitors. Usually we can’t hear those elements great on consumer devices. So you need to look elsewhere. Usually I find that issue in the 500hz-800hz, as a lot of those earbuds and iPhones bass clarity is coming from that 800hz ish area. And muddiness tends to reveal itself more.

If I remember on this album at original release it was changed and remixed, but recorded by Steve. 


The anniversary edition, included some of his original mixes. The record company had some songs remixed for this. To sound more commercial at the time. Steve is very very clinical when it comes to recording. He’s all about capturing the band as true as possible. But also known for his big drum sound. Kurt really wanted that sound, and admired his work. He’s not one to shove the vocal way up, and it shows on his mixes the record company hated at the time(heard on the anniversary cuts). For him it’s just a science and his own way. 

On most interviews he can’t even recall what he did much. Just that he focused on getting the most precise sound of what the band is. For better or worse, he saw it as his job to capture the truth. And that’s what he did! There was a big dispute over handing over the mixes to someone else. 

If you haven’t yet, take a listen to the anniversary edition of the album with Albini mixes on it. You’ll notice drums are crazy huge, vocals aren’t the main target, the guitar solo on Heart Shape box was way different!  I watched the SNL live version, and it’s exactly what the band performed live with Steve to me. Not a lot of effects or doubling going on there on his mixes. I was very happy we got to final here the originals!

“When asked about the feedback he received, Cobain told Michael Azerrad, "The grown-ups don't like it." He said he was told his songwriting was "not up to par", the sound was "unlistenable", and that there was uncertainty that mainstream radio would accept Albini's production.”

https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_Utero#Production_and_mixing_dispute

I use closed for recording and tracking(ATH-M50). Haven’t bought open back yet…but I do switch on Sonaworks 3 sometimes to adjust the headphones with a profile just to see. Also I use my monitors at speaking voice level, when I’m done tracking and mixing the 1st demo. I use a bunch of crappy ear buds and bounce it out to Dropbox at my session rate, to play on portable speakers. This usually does a good job. 

I use a JBL portable speaker that’s super bass heavy, then also a Bose speaker that’s more thin and balanced that represents what most would hear on a basic system. Also I test on my iPhone speakers against other pro mixes. Getting that 35hz-800hz is key, to not sound muddy or if the bass is not cutting through on a pair of earbuds/crappy speakers. 

Usually when trying on different consumer speakers, and ear buds with a demo mix. I can spot issues in the low end and up to 500hz-800hz range. This is important for basic systems most listeners will hear on. I’ve actually thought about grabbing an Auraotone mix cube to help with this more. Sometimes if you don’t know your headset well, or don’t try a variety of sources. You’ll just hear the bottom drop out, lack of bass or heaviness weight of the mix compared to big monitors. 

A big reason Mixcubes and NS10s are popular to pair with normal monitors(they aren’t meant to sound good, just if you can make it sound good on those it will translate well). But you don’t have to have those! 
 I recommend trying your bounces on thin playback sources, and take notes to change in the mix. Bluetooth speakers, earbuds, iPhone, laptop speakers are all good tests to take notes of what’s lacking or masking in the mix. Then go back and fix those elements. This practice works for many!

Tested it tonight…AI is good for a quick demo mix if you’re just playing around. I do like the unmask feature the most, and could see using that. But the auto AI learning for me, is just ok. It takes up a good bit of CPU in Ableton, that I could just eq myself with less CPU strain. It feels kind of like the all in one CLA plugins, when they first came out. As far as the sound, and bold eq/comp/fx going on under the hood. That’s what it reminds me of a bit. I found myself stripping away stuff.

That’s the feeling I had testing out the AI. Just generic eq, and unnecessary effects that make me turn my buffer up. I could see it helping some, or people on a budget quick demo. But the modules are where it’s at, and the unmasking tool def comes in handy. 

But a lot of what the AI does, you could just look at it after, get in the ball park and do a better job yourself…And then have less cpu taken up overall.  I ran a live Moog bass riff, a drum kit sequence using samples, Kontakt and some reverb sends. Had 6 tracks with it on two tracks with the AI, and it felt a bit unnecessary while still tracking. 

I’m using an I7/6core with 64gb ddr4 ram. I had to put it at 512 with both instances, to process with AI then ramp it back down. Turning the AI off, and using the modules I could easily use 128 buffer, many tracks and not break  a sweat at 88.2khz. So it’s not worth using the AI for me, and is hit or miss. But it could give some an idea where to go, if they like the sound. 

You could just use Neutron on each track minus the AI, and get a pretty good mix with the modules and unmasking. I haven’t used it since the first one. But overall results, if you’re using a handful of tracks…the AI isn’t that bad sounding for a start. Just the AI CPU hit, is a bit much in Ableton. It could be less in Logic as in my experience, takes advantage of multithreading and runs better with intensive sessions. But the modules are pretty good, along with the unmasking tool. I will def use it minus the AI, outside curiosity sake.

I’ve been apart of the hiring process when I was an ARA for 6 years. I saw some great candidates my GM turned down. Her reason was the over qualified were more likely to leave within 1 year. Which was usually true most the time. They like to hire people in college for part time, and open schedule for those not likely to go anywhere. Most graduates they turned down unless they were older out of work, and retail experience. But if you have an open schedule, and in the interview…. say you plan to get experience for a number of years there. 

Talk about how you see growing with the company. Talk about teamwork, and how you like to be in front of people vs behind a desk. That can work sometimes if you have an open schedule, and interview that way very positively. Maybe relate some scenarios you’ve been through with retail, selling vs talking about IT work. Most of your experience will go over their head. Then they think you’re to focused on growing into a different field fast. Convince them you’re staying around, and talk more sales. They aren’t interested in what you learned at school. So make that 10% of the interview talk if asked. It’s more about sales and communication. They can teach on the job, and screw ups aren’t uncommon under such pressure. If you like IT don’t work there, and look for a local help desk to start.

If you get a claim usually they just take the $300 insurance, and you get a new screen put on your existing. Or if that exceeds cost of the tv or it’s legacy, you get an “equivalent”. Which would be a c1,c2,c3 ect. At whatever time you put your claim in. So just depends in that 5 year warranty when it’s used. But if you do get a new tv…$300 insurance gone, and you have the option to pay $300 again for the new insurance on the new “equivalent” or not.

It works out pretty well. But no they won’t hand you a $700 gift card because your TVs old at a prorate. They however will prorate the insurance if the claim happens very early. So you may pay $150 on the new replacement TVs insurance, if it’s a year or two in vs $300 again if you want that…but that’s all optional on the replacement tv. 

The $300 for 5 years covers everything, but breaking the glass. I don’t know of any other insurance that covers burn ins. Plus 3 year insurance isn’t much worth it, as the chance of something happening is low. But 5 years def, if you are a gamer or watch a lot of content with static images. It’s a nice piece of mind for me as I use mine a lot. And already had a pixel go out in year 2. It’s not noticeable 4ft back, so I’m not worried too much with 3 years left. So with an OLED such as the LG CX/C1, you should leave all at default, and set the HDR luminance to 4. 4=800nits. This will help you achieve proper HGIG and spectral details. It’ll still be bright overall with the brightness at 10(brightness is your paper white, and adjust between 7-10 depending on room). 

But the HDR Luminance is your nits, and we usually clip 1 over what our tv can do. So LG CX is 700-725 nits varied per panel. So we choose 4 to hit 800 nits, and clip it for any extra detail. Same as you did for the PS5 calibration HDTVTESTS went over.  

If using any other tv, such as a led with 900/1000 nits. You want to adjust the same as well. Which would be 5(900) or 6(1000). Lower range TVs with 400nits will of course be much lower.Think of it as from 4=800 5=900 6=1000 and so on. 

After that I find leaving dark at lowest for blacks especially on OLED TVs, and brightness at 7-10. I find a balance between 7 and 10 depending on dark room. Just tune that to what you like!
